name: [BUAMS] KUL 5 SELF REGULATED LEARNING (YOS)
text:
Yossi Indra Kusuma, S.Ked., M.Med.Ed.
Self-Directed
• Taking initiative without 
assistance
• Diagnosing own needs 
(Nilson, 2016)
• Formulate own learning 
journey
• Evaluate own learning 
(Gibbons, 2002)
Self-Regulated
• Reduces instructional time
• Manage learning and time 
efficiently (Yang, 1993)
• Ivolves agency, purpose, 
perceptions (Zimmerman, 
1989)
• Tied to student efficacy 
(Pintrich, 1990)
SELF-EFFICACY
One’s own capabilities to organize and implement actions 
to attain success (Bandura, 1989). Work harder, persist 
longer; achieve higher levels (Zimmerman, 1991)
Introduction
• The challenge for the teachers is how to help the students learn 
intentionally, autonomously and effectively
• The use of learning strategies is crucial for students academic performance 
and promoting deeper learning approaches
• The SRL models offer comprehensive theoretical backgrounds, it enable 
more holistic approaches to the use of learning strategies
• There are differences in key self-regulation processes between high and 
low achieving learners and performers
Theoretical Principal
• Winne‟s model (1996, 1997) is highly cognitive (information 
processing approaches), Zimmerman‟s model comes from social-
cognitive theory and Boekaerts‟ model (1999) is more situated 
(exploring the influence of the context in the type of goals the 
students pursue)
• All these theories share the common ground that self-regulation is 
composed of different processes (e.g., monitoring, goal setting, 
etc.) and it is cyclical, meaning that each performance of the task 
provides feedback for the strategy used in future tasks
Three important characteristics across the various theories : 
Goal-directed behaviour
 The adaptation and 
modification to one’s 
behaviours or strategies 
to optimise learning
Use of specific strategies 
to attain goals
• Many theorists emphasise the role of metacognitive control and self-
monitoring as students learn or perform (Winne & Hadwin 1998; 
Zimmerman 2000). 
• Metacognition (thinking about thinking) is one’s knowledge concerning 
own cognitive processes - learning-relevant properties of information (Flavell, 
1996)
• The extent to which students can skilfully observe, or notice, when 
learning is successful or not and then to identify the contributing 
conditions or factors influencing that learning is a key regulation 
process
How to be more Metacognitive???
1. How do I know when I know something?
2. What is the evidence and how reliable is it?
3. How the events, theories, models, people connected?
4. What is the cause and effect?
5. What is new and ols-have you run across this idea 
before? When, where, what did it mean and how can 
your further connect it now?
6. So what? Why does it matter? What does it all mean?
BENEFIT
Self-regulation theory offers an exciting potential for 
improving academic and clinical performance in 
medical education
Definition
• Self-generated thoughts, feelings, and actions that are planned and 
cyclically adapted to the attainment of personal goals (Zimmerman, 2000)
• The cyclical control of academic and clinical performance through several 
key processes that include goal-directed behaviour, use of specific 
strategies to attain goals, and the adaptation and modification to 
behaviours or strategies to optimise learning and performance.
• Super ordinate process characterised by various sub-processes, such as 
goal-setting, planning, strategy use, self-control, self-monitoring and 
self-reflection (Puustinen & Pulkkinen 2001)
Self-regulation is the control that students have 
over their cognition, behaviour, emotions and 
motivation through the use of personal 
strategies to achieve the goals they have 
established
Definition
• Control of cognition :  which it is the cognitive 
component of self-regulation also known as 
metacognition
• Behaviour control : it is needed to control what the 
student is actually doing to achieve the goals
Definition
• Emotion control : students experience emotions while performing 
academic tasks; thus, controlling the emotions is crucial, especially 
when the tasks could block the students’ performance (Boekaerts & 
Corno, 2005)
• Motivation control  : being aware of one‟s motivation and 
generating self-motivation, maintaining interest and attention during a 
task (Kuhl, 2000; Wolters, 2003)
SOCIAL COGNITIVE MODEL
• Individuals are active participants in their lives who seek control over 
important events through the regulation of their thoughts, actions and 
environmental factors to achieve personal goals (Bandura, 1986)
• Reciprocal interactions among behaviours, the environment and personal 
factors such as beliefs and affect
• This active process of making adjustments in the pursuit of personal goals 
is at the heart of self-regulation and is largely mediated by an individual’s 
self-beliefs and judgements, such as self-efficacy
Forethought phase (before)
•
It is the initial phase in which the students approach the task: analysing it, 
assessing their capacity to perform it with success and establishing goals and 
plans regarding how to complete it
•
The task interest and the goal orientation play a crucial role to achieve adequate 
planning and performing the task appropriately
•
Zimmerman (2000) argues that this preparatory phase underscores the proactive 
essence of self-regulated learners and that such preparatory thoughts and actions 
facilitate adaptive self-evaluation and reflection after learning has occurred
Forethought phase (2 main activities) :
• analyse what the task 
characteristics : by creating a first 
representation of how it should be 
performed
TASK ANALYSIS
• analyse the value the task : conditions 
their motivation and effort, and 
therefore the attention they will pay 
during the performance; in other 
words, their activation of self-
regulatory strategies
SELF-
MOTIVATION 
BELIEFS
TASK ANALYSIS
•
The task fragmented into smaller pieces and the personal strategies for the 
performance are chosen based on previous knowledge and/or experience
•
This is the phase in which the goals and strategic planning are established, 
which are key conditions for self-regulation to occur
•
The main differences between experts and novices, the former spending more 
time planning, which has shown to be crucial for their higher achievement
•
Two crucial variables when establishing their goals: the assessment criteria 
and the performance level they want to achieve
Beliefs, value, interest and goals
•
Are the personal variables that generate and maintain the motivation to 
perform a task
•
The motivation to perform a task is the result of the interaction of these 
variables
•
Self-efficacy expectations are beliefs about the personal capability to perform a 
task
•
Outcomes expectations are beliefs about the success of a given task
•
Interest and task value are variables that energise the students‟ initial approach 
to the task
•
Goal orientation which is the students belief about the purposes of their learning
Performance phase (During) :
• It is important that the students keep their concentration and that 
they use appropriate learning strategies for two reasons :
1.
So their motivation does not decrease
2.
To keep track of their progress towards their goals
• Two main processes during the performance are self-observation 
and self-control, and in order for them to work successfully a 
number of strategies can be followed
Self-observation
• A prerequisite to control the task process is that students have a 
clear understanding of the adequacy and quality of what they are 
doing, so if it is correct they can continue and if not they can 
change it.
• For students to self-observe successfully, there are two types of 
actions they can perform; one of a cognitive nature and the other of 
external help
Self-monitoring
• The first type of action is self-monitoring, also known as metacognitive 
monitoring or self-supervision
• Self-monitoring is compares what it is being done against criteria that 
assess the quality of the process being followed
• It is a similar process to self-assessment only in that this happens once the 
task has been finished and self-monitoring occurs during the performance
• This way as it is possible to have standards to assess the final “self-
assessment of the product” and it is possible to have standards 
regarding how to perform the task “self-assessment of the process.”
Self-recording
• Coding the actions that are being done during the performance
• Students can be aware of things that could have gone undetected 
before
• It is important to remember that during the performance, an overload 
of cognitive processing can happen impeding the mental 
registering of all the actions performed
Self-control
• Maintaining concentration and interest during performance it is 
not effortless, it actually requires the use of a series of strategies.
• The eight strategies that are presented next can be classified as 
metacognitive strategies (the first six) and motivational strategies 
(the last two), being that the purpose of the first ones is to maintain 
concentration and the purpose of the latter to maintain interest 
and motivation
Self-control (8 strategies)
1.
If the students have a clear understanding for the task, they can use 
specific strategies to perform the task (ex: underlining text while reading)
2.
Students can use self-instruction, which are self-directed orders or 
descriptions about the task that is being performed (ex: asking themselves 
during a math exercise about the steps to take and if they are correct)
3.
Students can use imagery, which is the use of mental images that 
organise the information and help to focus attention on enhancing learning 
and memorisation (ex: creating a concept map)
Self-control (8 strategies)
4.
Use time management, having a perspective of all the aspects of the task 
they need to perform (ex: is to set intermediate goals in the writing of, for 
example, a dissertation)
5.
To maintain the attention and interest in the task a structured learning 
environment is needed (ex: not to sit down by the side of a classmate who 
talks during class)
6.
Students experience blocks to their learning processes that can be solved 
through help seeking (e.g., asking the teacher how to solve a problem)
Self-control (8 strategies)
7.
The use of incentives to enhance or maintain their interest during 
the task. This is done through self-directing messages that remind 
them of the goal to achieve or the challenge they are trying to solve 
(ex: “I will find a way to solve this problem” or “I won‟t get distracted, 
it is important to understand this exercise.”)
8.
Use self-consequences to overcome feeling want to quit the task 
when does not experience progress (through self-praise and self-
rewards)
Self-reflection Phase (After) :
• Students judge their work and formulate reasons for their 
results
• While justifying their success or failure, they experience 
positive or negative emotions depending on their 
attributional style
• These emotions will influence their motivation and 
regulation in the future
Self-judgement
• Self-judgment is the process through which the students assess 
their performance : composed of self-evaluation and causal 
attribution
• Self evaluation : students assessment of their own performance 
based on the assessment criteria and modulated by their 
performance level goal (Panadero, 2011)
• Causal attributions are the explanations that students give to 
themselves about their success or failure in a task
 Judgment standards
• The ones in which students base their self evaluation and 
are influenced by the assessment criteria which can be 
established in three ways (Bandura, 1986)
1. Based on an analysis of the competence that the 
students are about to learn (objective criterion)
2. Based on previous performance levels (progress 
criterion)
3. Based on comparison with others‟ performance 
(social comparison criterion)
Self-reaction
• The students react emotionally and cognitively to their own 
attributions
• If students learn how to judge their success and failure as opportunities 
to improve and learn they can then control their attribution style so 
that it is more adaptive and, as a result, control better their emotions
• Zimmerman and Moylan (2009) pointed out that there are two processes 
that need to be taken into account when it comes to self-reaction: self 
satisfaction/affect and adaptive/defensive decisions
• Self-satisfaction is defined as the affective and cognitive reactions that 
students experience when they are judging themselves (Zimmerman & 
Moylan, 2009)
• Adaptive/defensive decisions : adaptive decisions, the willingness to 
perform the task again is maintained whether keeping the same strategies or 
using new ones to obtain better results. On the other hand, when defensive 
decisions are taken, students try to avoid performing the task again so as 
not to experience new failures (Wolters, 2003)
Effective learners have a small repertoire of favourite 
strategies that are ‘tried and trusted’ but 
underachieving learners either have a limited range of 
effective strategies or repeatedly use ineffective 
strategies
(Pressley & Ghatala 1990)
SRL PROMPTS (Alten, Phielix & Janssen, 2020)
PLANNING
What kind of task is this? How will I know I have reached 
my goal? How motivated am I? How much time will be 
necessary? What do I already know? What strategies 
should I use? What strengths can I bring? How can I 
compensate for my weakness?
SRL PROMPTS (Alten, Phielix & Janssen, 2020)
MONITORING
Am I sure I know what I am doing? Does my approach make sense? 
How well are my strategies working? Am I making good progress? 
What change should I make? What material is the most important? 
What material am I having trouble understanding? How does what I am 
learning relate to what I already know? How does it relate to my 
experience? How is my thinking on the topic changing?
SRL PROMPTS (Alten, Phielix & Janssen, 2020)
EVALUATING
How well did I achieve my goal? What approach worked 
well and what didn’t? What do I need to do differently? 
What am I still having trouble applying? What questions do 
I have? How does what I learned relate to other concepts?
References
• Sandars, J., & Cleary, T. J. (2011). Self-regulation theory: Applications to 
medical education: AMEE Guide No. 58. Medical Teacher, 33(11), 875–886. 
https://doi.org/10.3109/0142159X.2011.595434
• Panadero, E., & Alonso-Tapia, J. (2014). How do students self-regulate? 
Review of Zimmerman’s cyclical model of self-regulated learning. Anales de 
psicologia, 30(2), 450-462.
• van Alten, D. C., Phielix, C., Janssen, J., & Kester, L. (2020). Effects of self-
regulated learning prompts in a flipped history classroom. Computers in 
human behavior, 108, 106318.
